analysis.one_liner: Makes employers legally liable for workplace harassment by anyone who directs a worker's daily duties.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have restored a broader definition of "supervisor" for holding employers liable in harassment cases, never received a committee vote or floor vote and died when the 2019-21 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a 2013 Supreme Court decision (Vance v. Ball State University), employers can avoid being held responsible for harassment by someone who bosses a worker around day to day but cannot formally hire, fire, or demote them. This bill would change the law so that employers are liable for harassment by anyone authorized to direct a worker's daily work activities, or when employer negligence allowed a hostile environment to continue. It applies to discrimination based on sex, race, age, disability, and genetic information, and covers private employers and federal workplaces, including Congress's own offices.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are harassed by shift leads, crew chiefs, and other mid-level bosses who control their daily work but cannot formally hire or fire them — a group the bill's findings say is concentrated in restaurants, retail, health care, housekeeping, and personal care, and disproportionately includes women and people of color in low-wage jobs. Under current law, an employer can escape liability by pointing to the harasser's lack of formal hiring-and-firing power; the bill would close that route, making it easier for victims to win damages. It would also cover federal employees, including congressional staff.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers harassed by bosses who direct their daily work

how_it_helps.text: Restores the pre-2013 rule that an employer is responsible for harassment by anyone the employer authorized to direct the employee's daily work activities, not only someone with power to take formal actions like hiring and firing — reversing the Supreme Court's Vance v. Ball State University decision.

Adds a negligence route: an employer is liable when its own negligence let a hostile work environment be created or continue, so employers cannot escape responsibility simply because the harasser lacked a formal supervisor title.

Applies the new standard across the major federal anti-discrimination laws — covering sex, race, age, disability, and genetic-information discrimination — including for federal employees and congressional offices under the Congressional Accountability Act.
Applies to all claims pending on or after enactment, so workers with cases already in court would benefit immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Employers. Businesses and government workplaces would face a wider set of harassment claims and greater exposure to damages, settlements, and insurance costs, because harassers with day-to-day control over workers would now trigger employer liability even where the employer never knew about the conduct. Some of that cost is the point — it gives employers a financial reason to police harassment — but it also means more litigation expense for employers generally, including small businesses in the low-wage industries the bill names.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes what is effectively strict liability on employers for harassment by anyone authorized to direct a worker's daily duties, even if the employer exercised reasonable care to prevent and correct harassment and did not know about the conduct — unlike the negligence-based part of the standard, this branch of liability does not depend on employer fault.

Broader employer liability means more harassment litigation and higher legal, settlement, and insurance costs for employers, which falls hardest on small businesses; the bill preserves existing legal defenses (Section 12) but does not cap exposure.
Applying the standard retroactively to all claims pending on or after enactment changes the rules for lawsuits already underway, which employers would reasonably object to.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the upside is concrete: the 2013 Supreme Court decision narrowed who counts as a "supervisor," and workers whose day-to-day boss is not the person who signs off on hires and firings currently have a weaker claim — a gap the bill's own findings tie to restaurants, retail, health care, housekeeping, and personal care, where many workers are women and people of color in low-wage jobs. The cost is real but limited: employers face wider liability and litigation expense, with the fault-free branch of the standard being the most debatable design choice. On balance the bill shifts the cost of harassment back onto the workplaces that benefit from workers' labor, which is a deliberate policy trade, not a drafting flaw — though a narrower, negligence-only standard would have balanced the two interests more gently.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees, then to a Judiciary subcommittee, and no committee ever voted on it or scheduled it for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on July 25, 2019, joined by six Democratic cosponsors.

The same day, the Speaker referred it to four committees — Education and Labor, House Administration, Judiciary, and Oversight and Reform — meaning any one of them could have acted on it, but all of them had to weigh in first for the parts in their jurisdiction.
On August 15, 2019, the Judiciary Committee referred it to its Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, which was the bill's last action.
No hearing, markup, or vote in any committee followed, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers — including businesses in low-wage industries and the government workplaces the bill covered — are better off, because the broader harassment liability standard it would have imposed never took effect. The congressional offices the bill would have regulated under the Congressional Accountability Act also avoided the change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that avoided broader harassment liability

against.name: Chairs of the House Education and Labor, House Administration, Judiciary, and Oversight and Reform Committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill in any of the four committees to which it was referred; the last action was a subcommittee referral in August 2019

against.name: Business and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Have historically opposed legislation restoring the broader harassment liability standard this bill would reinstate

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill (1 sponsor and 6 cosponsors, all Democrats), but no vote was ever recorded in committee or on the floor, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Employers in low-wage service industries (restaurants, retail, health care, housekeeping, personal care)
industries.note: The bill's findings single out these industries as places where workers are often bossed day-to-day by people without formal hiring-and-firing power, so the expanded liability standard would bite hardest here. Employers would face more harassment claims and settlement costs, which is exactly the deterrent the bill intends.
Every employer covered by Title VII, the ADEA, the ADA, and related laws would face a wider definition of supervisors who trigger automatic liability, increasing litigation and insurance exposure.

industries.industry: Federal government and Congress as employer
industries.note: The bill applies the same standard to federal agencies, the Smithsonian, executive-branch offices, and congressional employing offices under the Congressional Accountability Act, so lawmakers' own staff would gain the same protection as private-sector workers.

industries.industry: Employment defense law firms and employment practices liability insurers
industries.note: More harassment claims and broader employer exposure mean more litigation work and higher premiums, a secondary economic effect of the liability shift.
